I am a 61-year-old farmer in Quzhou, and I have been working this land for 40 years. My father taught me, and I have watched the fields change with the weather every year. I know this soil like I know my own hands. My farm is 7.8 mu, and I grow wheat and maize in rotation — that is the way here on the North China Plain. With only my wife and me at home now, I cannot afford to waste labor or money, but I also cannot afford a bad harvest.

For the wheat, I will plant the whole 7.8 mu in autumn with an improved variety — maybe something like Jimai 22 or what the seed station recommends this year. I trust the improved seeds because they resist lodging better than the old kinds, and at my age I cannot afford to lose a crop to wind. I will plough the field first to bury the maize stubble and break the hardpan, then rotary till to make a good seedbed. For fertilizer, I will put down compound fertilizer as a base, then top-dress with urea at green-up and jointing. In total, I use about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, 6 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium — that is what this soil needs after all these years. I irrigate three times: once before winter to help the seedlings survive the cold, once at jointing when the wheat is hungry for water, and once at flowering to fill the grain. I spray pesticide once or twice if I see aphids or rust, but I do not spray for nothing. I expect about 480 kg per mu from the wheat if the spring rains do not fail.

After the wheat harvest in early June, I immediately plant maize on the same 7.8 mu. I use hybrid seed — the yield is too good to ignore, and everyone around here uses it now. I do not plough after wheat; I plant no-tillage directly into the stubble to save time and keep moisture in the ground. The soil is already loose from the wheat season. For fertilizer, I spread compound fertilizer at planting and side-dress urea when the maize is knee-high. In total, about 15 kg nitrogen per mu, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium. I irrigate twice if it is dry: once when the maize is jointing, and once at tasseling and silking — that is the most critical time. I spray pesticide two or three times because the corn borer and armyworm have been worse these past years. I expect about 580 kg per mu if the summer storms come right.

I keep some grain for our own food and sell the rest. With only two of us, we do not need much, but we need cash for medicine and daily expenses. I do what the land tells me, and after 40 years, it usually tells me the truth.
